overview: A Composite Index (multi-column index) is an index built on two or more columns, where the index entries are sorted first by the leading column, then by the next, and so on.
Its usefulness is governed by the leftmost-prefix rule: a query can use the index only if it filters on a contiguous leftmost set of the index's columns starting from the first one.

Column order is the single most important design choice: put equality predicates before range predicates, order leading columns by selectivity and query usage, and exploit covering potential to avoid lookups.
learningObjectives: Understand how a composite index sorts entries by column order and why that order dictates which queries it can serve.
Master the leftmost-prefix rule and the equality-before-range guidance for ordering columns.
Determine when a query can or cannot use a composite index and how to make composite indexes covering.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A composite index is a B-tree index keyed on an ordered list of two or more columns (c1, c2, ..., cn). Index entries are sorted lexicographically by that column order. The index can satisfy predicates that form a leftmost prefix of the key (c1, then c1+c2, etc.), and can perform efficient range scans only on the last column referenced after all preceding columns are matched by equality.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine a phone book sorted by last name, then first name. You can find everyone with last name 'Smith', and within that everyone named 'Smith, John'. But you cannot efficiently find everyone whose first name is 'John' regardless of last name, because the book is not organized that way. A composite index is sorted by column order in exactly this manner, and that order decides which lookups are fast.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Multi-column indexes have been part of relational systems since their inception, but the practical 'leftmost-prefix' rule became a staple of database tuning literature as engineers learned that column order, not just column choice, determines index usability. MySQL's documentation and SQL Server tuning guides codified equality-before-range and prefix rules that remain core interview material today.

whyItMatters.business: Correctly ordered composite indexes turn multi-condition searches and sorted reports into fast seeks, improving the responsiveness of the features users rely on most.
whyItMatters.engineering: Composite indexes can replace several single-column indexes, reducing write overhead while serving complex predicates; getting the column order right is a high-leverage tuning skill.
whyItMatters.scalability: By matching the dominant multi-column query pattern, a single composite index keeps query cost proportional to matched rows as data grows, instead of scanning.
whyItMatters.cost: One well-ordered composite (often covering) index reduces both the number of indexes to maintain and the I/O per query, lowering storage and compute spend.
whyItMatters.reliability: Predictable seek behavior depends on understanding which queries the index can serve; misordered columns cause silent fallbacks to scans and unpredictable latency.

coreComponents.name: Leading (First) Column
coreComponents.definition: The first column in the index key, which the entire index is primarily sorted by.
coreComponents.purpose: It is the most important column for usability; the index is only seekable when a query filters on this column.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Anchors the leftmost prefix; usually the most frequently filtered and/or most selective equality column.
coreComponents.examples: In an index on (tenant_id, created_at), tenant_id is the leading column.

coreComponents.name: Subsequent (Trailing) Columns
coreComponents.definition: The columns after the leading column, used to break ties within each value of the preceding columns.
coreComponents.purpose: To refine the search and support range scans or sorting once preceding columns are matched by equality.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Provide additional filtering/sorting only when all preceding key columns are constrained.
coreComponents.examples: created_at in (tenant_id, created_at) supports time ranges within a tenant.

coreComponents.name: Column Order (Key Order)
coreComponents.definition: The defined left-to-right sequence of columns that determines the sort order of index entries.
coreComponents.purpose: To control which predicate combinations can use the index and which range/sort operations are efficient.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Embodies the leftmost-prefix rule and equality-before-range guidance; the primary tuning lever.
coreComponents.examples: (status, region) versus (region, status) serve different queries despite the same columns.

internalWorking: The index stores entries sorted by the full key tuple: first by c1, then by c2 within equal c1, then by c3, and so on, exactly like multi-level alphabetical ordering.

A seek matches columns left to right by equality; once it reaches a column used with a range (>, <, BETWEEN, LIKE 'prefix%'), it can range-scan that column but the columns to its right are no longer in usable sorted order for further seeking.
If a query omits the leading column, the index entries are not sorted by the columns it does filter on, so the engine cannot seek and typically falls back to a scan (or ignores the index).
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Predicate (c1=, c2=, c3 range) -> Seek c1 -> within c1 Seek c2 -> within c2 Range-Scan c3 -> Leaf entries -> [if covered] Result, else Lookup
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. Index defined on (tenant_id, status, created_at); query: WHERE tenant_id = 7 AND status = 'open' AND created_at >= '2026-01-01'.
2. The engine seeks tenant_id = 7, then within those seeks status = 'open' (both equality), landing on a contiguous block.
3. Within that block, entries are sorted by created_at, so it range-scans created_at >= '2026-01-01' efficiently.
4. A different query WHERE status = 'open' (omitting tenant_id) cannot use this index for a seek because status is not a leftmost prefix, so the optimizer scans instead.

keyTerminology.meaning: A composite index can be used only for predicates that form a contiguous prefix of its key starting from the first column (c1, then c1+c2, then c1+c2+c3).
keyTerminology.importance: It is the central rule that determines whether a query can use a composite index at all.

keyTerminology.meaning: Guidance to place equality-predicate columns before range-predicate columns in the key, because a range column 'stops' further seekable use of trailing columns.
keyTerminology.importance: Maximizes the number of key columns that can be used for an efficient seek.

keyTerminology.meaning: An optimizer technique (in some engines) that can use a composite index even when the leading column is not filtered, by probing each distinct leading value, viable only when the leading column has low cardinality.
keyTerminology.importance: A nuanced exception to the leftmost-prefix rule worth knowing for advanced interviews.

importantConcepts.explanation: Once a column is used with a range predicate, columns after it in the key cannot be used for further seeking because, within the range, entries are not sorted by the trailing columns. This is why a trailing range column should generally be the last useful key column.

A composite index can satisfy an ORDER BY without a separate sort if the ORDER BY columns match a leftmost prefix of the key (in compatible direction), because the index already stores rows in that order.

variationsAndTypes: **Equality-Only Composite Index:** All key columns used with equality, e.g., (country, city) for exact-match lookups.
**Equality-Then-Range Composite Index:** Leading equality columns followed by a trailing range column, e.g., (customer_id, order_date) for a customer's orders in a date range.
**Covering Composite Index:** A composite key plus INCLUDE columns so the query is served entirely from the index.
**Composite Unique Index:** Enforces uniqueness across the combination of columns, e.g., UNIQUE (tenant_id, email).
advantages: **Serves Multi-Column Predicates:** A single index satisfies queries filtering on several columns at once.
**Replaces Multiple Indexes:** Often substitutes for several single-column indexes, cutting write and storage overhead.
**Supports Sorted Output:** Can satisfy ORDER BY on a leftmost prefix without an extra sort.
**Covering Potential:** With the right column order and INCLUDE, it can fully cover complex queries.
disadvantages: **Order-Dependent Usability:** Wrong column order makes the index useless for important queries (leftmost-prefix rule).
**Limited Flexibility:** It cannot efficiently serve a query that filters only on a non-leading column.
**Wider Keys:** More key columns mean larger index entries and more write maintenance.
**Easy to Misdesign:** Subtle ordering mistakes (range before equality) silently degrade performance.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use a composite index when queries consistently filter (or filter and sort) on the same set of columns; order columns by equality-first then range, and by selectivity/usage among equality columns.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid composite indexes when the columns are queried independently in many different combinations (single-column or differently ordered indexes may serve better), or when the leading column is rarely filtered.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: A composite index is like a library catalog sorted by genre, then author, then title. You can quickly find all 'Science Fiction', then 'Science Fiction by Asimov', then a specific Asimov title. But if you only know a title and not the genre, the catalog's ordering does not help you find it directly, just as a query that skips the leading column cannot use the index.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A composite index on (A, B) also works like a separate index on B.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It does not. Because entries are sorted by A first, the index cannot seek on B alone; only a leftmost prefix (A, or A+B) is usable for seeking.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Column order in a composite index does not matter as long as the right columns are included.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Order is critical. (status, created_at) and (created_at, status) serve completely different queries; equality-before-range and selectivity drive the correct order.

productionConsiderations.scalability: A composite index aligned to the dominant query pattern keeps cost proportional to matched rows at scale; misaligned order forces scans that worsen as the table grows.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Predictable seeks depend on queries respecting the leftmost prefix; document the supported access patterns so application queries stay aligned and statistics stay fresh.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Like all indexes, composite indexes are derived and can be rebuilt from base data, so corruption is recoverable without data loss.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Watch for plans that scan despite an existing composite index, which usually signals a leftmost-prefix or column-order mismatch with the query.
productionConsiderations.security: Covering composite indexes copy INCLUDE columns into the index, so sensitive columns added for coverage must be classified and protected like the base data.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Consolidating several single-column indexes into one well-ordered composite index reduces storage and write overhead; drop redundant indexes whose prefix is covered by a composite.
productionConsiderations.performance: Order equality columns before range columns, choose the most useful leading column, align ORDER BY with the key prefix, and add INCLUDE columns to cover hot queries.

codeExamples.title: Leftmost-Prefix Rule in Action
codeExamples.overview: A composite index on (tenant_id, status, created_at) and which queries can or cannot use it as a seek.
codeExamples.breakdown: The index is sorted by tenant_id, then status, then created_at. Queries that constrain a leftmost prefix (tenant_id; tenant_id+status; tenant_id+status+created_at) get efficient seeks. Filtering on status alone skips the leading column, so no seek. Filtering on tenant_id and created_at while skipping status seeks only on tenant_id and then must scan/residual-filter created_at because status sits between them in the key.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Execution plans show Index Seek for the leftmost-prefix queries, a Scan (or ignored index) for the status-only query, and a seek on tenant_id followed by a residual predicate for the query that skips status.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Engineers expect the index to help a status-only filter and are surprised by a scan; they forget the leading column must be present for a seek.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: If status-only queries are common, either reorder columns or add a separate index; if (tenant_id, created_at) without status is common, consider an index in that order.

codeExamples.title: Equality-Before-Range and Covering
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrating why equality columns must precede range columns, and making the index covering.
codeExamples.code:
-- BAD order: range column (order_date) before equality column (customer_id).
-- Within the date range, entries are NOT sorted by customer_id,
-- so the customer_id equality cannot be used as a seek prefix.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Bad_date_customer
    ON Orders (order_date, customer_id);

-- GOOD order: equality (customer_id) first, range (order_date) last,
-- and INCLUDE output columns to make it covering.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Good_customer_date
    ON Orders (customer_id, order_date)
    INCLUDE (total_amount, status);

-- Served by a single seek + range scan, no key lookup, no sort:
SELECT customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status
FROM Orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
  AND order_date >= ''2026-01-01''
ORDER BY order_date;
codeExamples.breakdown: With (order_date, customer_id) the engine can range-scan order_date but cannot seek customer_id within that range. With (customer_id, order_date) it seeks customer_id = 42 by equality, then range-scans order_date, and because entries within a customer are sorted by order_date, the ORDER BY is satisfied with no sort. INCLUDE adds total_amount and status so the query is fully covered.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: The good index produces a single Index Seek with a range on order_date, no Key Lookup, and no Sort operator; the bad index forces a scan or an inefficient plan for the same query.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Placing the range column first is a frequent error that quietly disables the equality seek and forces extra work.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Always order equality predicate columns before the single range/sort column, and put output-only columns in INCLUDE to cover the query.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A multi-tenant analytics product runs a hot query for each tenant: 'show this tenant's open tickets created since a date, sorted by creation time'. The query was scanning a large shared Tickets table and was slow under load.
endToEndExample.inputData: Tickets table with tenant_id, status, created_at, subject, priority, and millions of rows across many tenants. The dominant query filters tenant_id (equality), status (equality), created_at (range), and sorts by created_at.
endToEndExample.architecture: A single shared Tickets table. The team designs one composite covering index aligned to the dominant multi-column query pattern instead of several single-column indexes.
processingSteps: 1. Identify predicates and sort: tenant_id =, status =, created_at range and ORDER BY created_at.
2. Apply equality-before-range: order equality columns tenant_id and status first, then the range/sort column created_at.
3. Order the two equality columns by usage/selectivity: tenant_id leads because every query filters by tenant.
4. Add INCLUDE (subject, priority) so the SELECT list is fully covered and no key lookup is needed.
5. Validate the plan: seek on tenant_id + status, range scan on created_at, no sort (ORDER BY aligns with the key), no key lookup.
endToEndExample.output: A single composite covering index on (tenant_id, status, created_at) INCLUDE (subject, priority) that serves the hot query with one seek, a range scan, no sort, and no lookup.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Track whether the hot query's plan stays a seek; alert on regressions to scans, which usually mean a query started skipping the leading column or statistics went stale.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If a new query variant filters on status without tenant_id, add a targeted index rather than reordering and breaking the existing hot path; refresh statistics after large data growth.
endToEndExample.finalResult: The per-tenant ticket query dropped from a large table scan to a narrow seek-and-range-scan that returns pre-sorted, fully covered rows, dramatically reducing latency and I/O while replacing several would-be single-column indexes with one.

industryUseCases.problem: Every query is scoped to a tenant and then filters/sorts by status or time within that tenant.
industryUseCases.solution: A composite index leading with tenant_id, then status, then a time column, covering the display fields.
industryUseCases.benefits: Tenant-scoped queries become narrow seeks, isolating tenants' performance and avoiding full-table scans.

industryUseCases.problem: Customers view their own orders within a date range, sorted by date.
industryUseCases.solution: A composite index on (customer_id, order_date) INCLUDE (total_amount, status) following equality-before-range.
industryUseCases.benefits: One seek plus range scan returns sorted, covered results with no key lookup or extra sort.

industryUseCases.problem: Queries fetch events for a specific device over a time window, ordered by time.
industryUseCases.solution: A composite index on (device_id, event_ts) so a device's events are contiguous and time-ordered.
industryUseCases.benefits: Efficient windowed reads per device and ORDER BY satisfied directly from the index.

productionDeepDive.scalability: A composite index matching the dominant query keeps cost proportional to matched rows even as the table reaches billions of rows; the leading column (e.g., tenant_id or device_id) effectively partitions the search space.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Composite indexes are derived structures, rebuildable from base data, so corruption is recoverable by rebuild and they introduce no independent data-loss risk.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Composite indexes replicate with the data; consolidating several single-column indexes into one composite reduces replication payload and write amplification across replicas.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Because they can be rebuilt from base tables, recovery plans may restore data first and rebuild composite indexes afterward, reducing backup size and restore time.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Order columns equality-before-range, lead with the most-used/most-selective equality column, align ORDER BY to a key prefix to avoid sorts, and INCLUDE output columns to cover hot queries; verify with execution plans.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Replace multiple overlapping single-column indexes with one well-ordered composite index to cut storage and write overhead; drop indexes whose leftmost prefix is already covered by the composite.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: INCLUDE columns physically duplicate data into the index; sensitive output columns added for coverage must be protected and classified the same as the base columns.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Capture plans for hot queries to confirm seeks, watch for residual predicates indicating a skipped middle column, and review missing/unused-index DMVs to refine column order.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Composite unique indexes enforce multi-column uniqueness (e.g., one email per tenant); consistency checks validate the index B-tree against base data.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Alert when a hot query's plan regresses from a composite-index seek to a scan, which typically indicates a query change, a leftmost-prefix violation, or stale statistics.

recommendedPractices: **Apply the Leftmost-Prefix Rule:** Ensure the index leads with the columns your hot queries always filter on.
**Equality Before Range:** Place equality-predicate columns first and the single range/sort column last in the key.
**Order Leading Columns by Usage and Selectivity:** Lead with the column that is always filtered and ideally most selective.
**Make Hot Queries Covering:** Use INCLUDE for output-only columns so the composite index serves the query without lookups.
engineeringStandards: Document the exact query pattern (predicates and sort) each composite index is designed to serve.
Review column order against the leftmost-prefix rule before deploying any composite index.
Consolidate redundant single-column indexes whose prefix a composite index already covers.
designRecommendations: Design one composite index per dominant multi-column access pattern rather than indexing every column separately.
Align the index key's leading columns with the most common WHERE and ORDER BY combination.
Limit the number of key columns; push purely output columns into INCLUDE to keep the key narrow.
namingConventions: Name composite indexes listing the key columns in order, e.g., IX_Tickets_tenant_status_created.
Reflect covering intent when useful, e.g., IX_Orders_customer_date_covering.
documentationStandards: Record the column order rationale (which equality columns, which range column).
List INCLUDE columns and note any sensitive data they duplicate.
Document which queries the index supports and which it deliberately does not.
testingStrategies: Verify via execution plans that target queries get seeks and that ORDER BY needs no sort.
Test queries that skip the leading or a middle column to confirm understood fallback behavior.
Benchmark replacing several single-column indexes with one composite to quantify write/storage savings.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting a range column before an equality column.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Designers order columns by intuition or alphabetically rather than by predicate type.
commonMistakes.impact: The equality column after the range can no longer be used for seeking, so the index seeks less and may scan, defeating its purpose.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Always order equality-predicate columns before the single range/sort column in the composite key.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting a composite index on (A, B) to serve a query that filters only on B.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Misunderstanding the leftmost-prefix rule; assuming any included column is independently seekable.
commonMistakes.impact: The optimizer cannot seek on B alone and scans, so a query that should be fast is slow.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Lead with the column queries always filter on, or add a separate index for the B-only access pattern (or use skip scan only if A has low cardinality).

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing the wrong leading column for the dominant query.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The most selective column is chosen as the lead even when many queries do not filter on it.
commonMistakes.impact: Queries that omit that leading column cannot use the index, so the most common access pattern falls back to scans.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Lead with the column present in (nearly) all hot queries, then order remaining equality columns by selectivity, then the range column.

comparisonSection.optionB: Two Single-Column Indexes on A and B
comparisonSection.explanation: A composite index efficiently serves predicates on A and on A+B and can avoid a sort on an (A, B) ORDER BY. Two separate indexes serve A and B independently and may be combined via an index intersection, but that is usually less efficient than a single ordered composite for the combined predicate.

These serve different queries despite the same columns. (status, created_at) helps WHERE status = ? AND created_at range, while (created_at, status) helps a created_at range first; choosing the wrong order makes the index useless for the intended query under the leftmost-prefix rule.

Putting equality columns first lets the engine seek through all of them and then range-scan the last column, maximizing seekable key columns. A leading range column stops further seekable use, so columns after it cannot be used as a seek prefix.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is a composite index?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A composite index is an index built on two or more columns, with entries sorted by the first column, then the second within equal first values, and so on. It serves queries that filter on those columns in left-to-right order.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Anchor the answer on the multi-level sort order, like a phone book sorted by last name then first name.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the leftmost-prefix rule?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A composite index can be used for a seek only when the query filters on a contiguous leftmost prefix of the key, starting from the first column. So an index on (A, B, C) can serve predicates on A, on A+B, or on A+B+C, but not on B alone or C alone.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: This is the single most-asked composite-index concept; tie it directly to the sort order of the key.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why should equality columns come before range columns in a composite index?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Because once a column is used with a range predicate, the entries within that range are not sorted by the columns to its right, so those trailing columns cannot be used for further seeking. Putting equality columns first lets the engine seek through all of them and then range-scan the final column, maximizing the seekable prefix.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Give a concrete example like (customer_id, order_date) versus (order_date, customer_id).

intermediateQuestions.question: Does an index on (A, B) help a query that filters only on B? Why or why not?
intermediateQuestions.answer: No, not for a seek. The index is sorted by A first, so entries for a given B value are scattered across all A values and are not contiguous. Without constraining A, the engine cannot seek on B and will typically scan. (Some engines may use an index skip scan if A has very low cardinality.)
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Mention the skip-scan exception as a nuance but stress the general rule.

advancedQuestions.question: How does a composite index let a query avoid a sort, and what are the conditions?
advancedQuestions.answer: If the query's ORDER BY columns match a leftmost prefix of the index key in a compatible direction, and the preceding key columns are constrained by equality, the index already stores rows in the requested order, so the engine can return them without a separate sort operator. For example, (customer_id, order_date) satisfies WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY order_date with no sort.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Connect the sort elimination to the index's physical ordering and the equality constraint on leading columns.

advancedQuestions.question: When would you prefer two single-column indexes over one composite index, or vice versa?
advancedQuestions.answer: Prefer one composite index when queries consistently filter on the same column combination (especially with a sort), because it gives a single efficient seek and can be covering. Prefer separate single-column indexes when the columns are queried independently in many different combinations, since a composite index only serves leftmost prefixes and would not help queries that lead with the trailing column.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Mention that index intersection of two single-column indexes is possible but usually less efficient than a tailored composite.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: You have an index on (order_date, customer_id). The hot query is WHERE customer_id = 42 AND order_date >= '2026-01-01' ORDER BY order_date, and it is slow. Why, and how do you fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The leading column is order_date used as a range, so customer_id (equality) sits after a range column and cannot be used as a seek prefix; the engine range-scans many dates and residually filters customer_id. The fix is to reorder per equality-before-range.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Create an index on (customer_id, order_date): customer_id equality is sought first, then order_date is range-scanned, and since rows within a customer are sorted by order_date the ORDER BY needs no sort. Add INCLUDE for the SELECT columns to make it covering. This turns a broad range scan with residual filtering into a precise seek.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design the indexing for a multi-tenant SaaS table where nearly every query is scoped to tenant_id and then filters by status and a time range, often sorted by time. Minimize the number of indexes.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Create one composite index leading with tenant_id (present in all queries), then status (equality), then created_at (range and sort), with INCLUDE columns for the display fields. This single index serves tenant-only, tenant+status, and tenant+status+time-range queries via leftmost prefixes and satisfies ORDER BY created_at without a sort.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: One composite index covers several access patterns and reduces write overhead versus multiple single-column indexes, but it cannot serve queries that filter on status or created_at without tenant_id; those need separate indexes. A wider key with INCLUDE increases index size.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Lead with the partitioning-like column (tenant_id) to bound each query's search space, monitor plans to confirm seeks, add targeted indexes only for proven non-prefix access patterns, and keep statistics fresh as tenants and data grow.

Can a composite index be covering, and how do INCLUDE columns interact with the key?
What is index intersection and when does the optimizer use it?
How does a leading range column limit the usefulness of trailing columns?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: A composite index keys on multiple columns sorted left-to-right; it is usable only for leftmost-prefix predicates, so column order is everything.
keyConcepts: Leftmost-prefix rule: must filter from the first column rightward.
Equality-before-range: equality columns first, range/sort column last.
A range column stops seekable use of columns after it.
ORDER BY on a key prefix avoids a sort.
Add INCLUDE columns to make the composite index covering.
commands: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Tickets_tenant_status_created ON Tickets (tenant_id, status, created_at);
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_customer_date ON Orders (customer_id, order_date) INCLUDE (total_amount, status);
CREATE UNIQUE NONCLUSTERED INDEX UX_Users_tenant_email ON Users (tenant_id, email);
interviewPoints: Leftmost-prefix rule is the #1 concept to state clearly.
Column order changes which queries the index serves.
Equality columns before the single range/sort column.
(A, B) does not help a B-only filter (except skip scan).
Composite + INCLUDE can cover and remove sorts and lookups.
quickNotes: Lead with the column present in (nearly) all hot queries.
Among equality columns, order by selectivity after usage.
A leading range column disables seeking on trailing columns.
(status, created_at) and (created_at, status) serve different queries.
One good composite index can replace several single-column indexes.

keyTakeaways: A composite index sorts entries by its columns left-to-right, so its usability is governed by the leftmost-prefix rule: a query must filter on a contiguous prefix starting at the first column to get a seek.

Column order is the dominant design decision; place equality-predicate columns before the single range/sort column so the engine can seek through all equality columns and then range-scan the last one.

An index on (A, B) cannot seek a query that filters only on B because entries are sorted by A first; such access patterns need a different leading column or a separate index (skip scan is a low-cardinality exception).
A composite index whose key prefix matches the ORDER BY can return rows pre-sorted with no sort operator, and adding INCLUDE columns makes it covering to eliminate key lookups.
One well-ordered composite index can replace several single-column indexes, reducing write and storage overhead while serving multi-column predicates efficiently at scale.
